pr_title: feat(compiler-cli): DI mode for ctors with default values
pr_body:
Previously, the AOT compiler would attempt to generate DI constructor calls for all constructors, and report errors if explicit type annotations or other problems prevented them from being generated.

This commit adds a new feature which specially handles constructors that have default values specificed for all parameters. When the compiler encounters such a constructor, it now generates a zero-arg constructor call (`new ClassName()`) as the factory function instead of a normal DI call. This means that the default values (the initializers) of all parameters will be used.

With this feature, the constructor form:

```typescript
constructor(foo = inject(FooService), bar = inject(BarService)) {}
```

now works correctly. Such a constructor can use DI in production, and have these default values overridden for tests.


Fixes #47606

Testing in Google's codebase reveals that:

1. Many existing components break, as they unnecessary initializers specified for constructor fields.
2. Many existing components also use this pattern in a semantically different way - they expect DI to work in production, and provide default values in tests.

We're going to take a step back and consider this design holistically, as more than just a minor feature of DI.

issue_context.title: Allow `inject()` usage as constructor parameter properties default
comments:
What happens to older code? It will be a breaking change, right? Or you are thinking about schematics that will handle the migration.
> What happens to older code? It will be a breaking change, right? Or you are thinking about schematics that will handle the migration.

Hey Santosh!
It shouldn't be a breaking change as traditional DI would still work. But it wouldn't work with tools that don't implement the transforms just like it already is today.

We only need to figure out a way to tell the compiler to skip DI when a parameter has a default value... except if Optional   or other decorators are used.
@yjaaidi I don't really like this idea. Let me explain:
1. once more you depend on the constructor. This makes things harder.
2. using this, you can only use TS privates, not true JS privates ( `#myThing = inject(MyThingService)` doesn't work in that context)
3. it is a workaround for a problem better solved than patched over.
4. introduces new issues, like figuring out how to be backward compatible.

The correct solution in my opinion would be to have a function that creates the injection context manually, especially during tests.
Not like testbed does it, but more dev/tool friendly:
for example:
```typescript
const testCmp = withContext(myCmp, providersArray)
```
A solution like that doesn't need any syntax/API changes in Angular and solves the problem for your tests.

EDIT:  Perhaps adding the used injectionTokens to the `reflectComponentType` will be useful for testing tools
Hi @SanderElias!

> once more you depend on the constructor. This makes things harder.

Sorry, I don't really get this. What do you mean?

> using this, you can only use TS privates, not true JS privates ( #myThing = inject(MyThingService) doesn't work in that context)
Agreed!

This might sound funny but personally, I am totally fine with using `inject` as a property initializer. I really like its simplicity, its versatility as we don't need any metadata or transformers + all the other advantages like type inference.
```ts
class {
  myService = inject(MyService);
}
```
I used to encourage people to keep using classic DI except for use cases like those described here https://marmicode.io/blog/angular-inject-and-injection-functions and here https://marmicode.io/blog/angular-private-services.
Since I realized that using `inject` is more versatile and makes things way easier when it comes to integrating new tools, I thought that I would try switching totally to `inject`.
In terms of testing, `TestBed` suits me fine as it can easily wrapped into something like this for convenience:
```ts
function createService(serviceType, providers) {
  TestBed.configureTestingModule({providers: [serviceType, ...providers]});
  return TestBed.inject(serviceType);
}
```

Now, in order to onboard more people in the `inject` adventure and observe its advantages & limitations on a larger scale, I realized that people needed something in between class DI & `inject`.
That's when I came up with this idea, thus the issue. I like to experiment with stuff on real apps with teams of different backgrounds then collect the feedback and see what provides the best DX instead of just using my own feelings & experience.

Even though it's not my favorite way of DI, there are some successful examples of the similar approach: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/

🤔 I am still wondering though... did I miss something or Angular is just ignored class level `design:paramtypes` typescript meta and manually creating the `ctorParameters` meta using custom transforms?
Is this just a legacy issue because we couldn't assume the availability of `emitDecoratorMetadata`? or something related to Closure & tsickle?

If Angular could use `design:paramtypes` (if it's not already, and then I wonder why it doesn't work with other tools) then there is no need for this 😆
... except for compat with tools not emitting meta like esbuild... which still seem to be an important reason
@yjaaidi 
Let me explain why it is harder when you depend on the constructor.
1. Inheritance (a bad idea to begin with, but DI makes it worse! (you need to chain yours deps up al the way))
2. You need one. People will put code in there that would be better off elsewhere. (ngOnint mostly)
3.  Readability. Especially when used with some of the options (`@skipself` `@host` and so on)
4. depends on parameter decorators. Those have a questionable future.
There are probably a couple more I missed.

Now, this:

>Now, in order to onboard more people in the inject adventure and observe its advantages & limitations on a larger scale, I realized that people needed something in between class DI & inject

My question is, why? 
Moving from the old way to the inject function is not that hard to teach, right?
Your proposal requires a breaking change to Agular. That might be fine if there is a _HUGE_ gain. 
All I see is a little convenience for those clamping to their old way of working. 
Or did I miss something in your proposal?

Hey @SanderElias,
> @yjaaidi Let me explain why it is harder when you depend on the constructor.
> 
> 1. Inheritance (a bad idea to begin with, but DI makes it worse! (you need to chain yours deps up al the way))
I totally agree with it being a bad idea 😉. By the way, you wouldn't have to chain the deps are they would all have a default value which is the one injected.
Though, for those who want to implement override the deps manually in this case, I agree with you, they will have to struggle and add optional parameters to chain to base:
```ts
class A {
 constructor(z = inject(Z)) {}
}

class B extends A{
  constructor(x = inject(X), y = inject(Y), z = undefined) {
    super(z);
  }
}
```
I'm not a big fan of this of course.

> 2. You need one. People will put code in there that would be better off elsewhere. (ngOnint mostly)

❤️ I love this one! Can't agree more!

> 3. Readability. Especially when used with some of the options (`@skipself` `@host` and so on)
> 4. depends on parameter decorators. Those have a questionable future.

With the `inject()` function, you won't need them as they would be options.
```ts
constructor(a = inject(A, {optional: true})) {}
```

>    There are probably a couple more I missed.

Here is another one which I find the most annoying by the way, parameters order! which is one of the worst implementation details.

Changing this:
```ts
constructor(baseUrl = inject(BASE_URL, {optional: true})) {} // bad idea btw, one should prefer a config service
```

to this:
```ts
constructor(locale = inject(LOCALE_ID), baseUrl = inject(BASE_URL, {optional: true})) {}
```

will not break any manual instantiation 😱... but crash at runtime (hopefully with some explicit noise).

> Now, this:
> 
> > Now, in order to onboard more people in the inject adventure and observe its advantages & limitations on a larger scale, I realized that people needed something in between class DI & inject
> 
> My question is, why? Moving from the old way to the inject function is not that hard to teach, right? Your proposal requires a breaking change to Agular. That might be fine if there is a _HUGE_ gain. All I see is a little convenience for those clamping to their old way of working. Or did I miss something in your proposal?

I am not sure that this would be a breaking change. It could probably coexist with traditional DI.
I think that we can assume that we should skip traditional DI for anything that has a default value if `@Optional()` is present.

I think that this is something in between. It's clearly not a huge gain and it's not just for those clamping to their old way of working.
While I don't personally need it and won't encourage my clients or community to use it, I still can hear and understand people who don't want to go through the `TestBed` overhead.
I could imagine someone implementing an alternative `TestBed` that could be faster or something... or there might also be use cases (testing or not) where one could take control of the DI.
That said, there could other ways of allowing this. For instance, it's already possible if one can dynamically replace `inject()` with a custom resolver. Or maybe hook in, in a different way that sets the current injector before instantiating stuff.
```ts
function createService(serviceType) {
  setInjector(myInjector)
  return new serviceType();
}
```

What do you think?

Maybe we should plan a call or an online community session or something... there is no rush though as this isn't crucial 😊
https://github.com/angular/angular-cli/issues/26323
Since we have a long way from that moment, now this is the issue with vite, which cannot pass variable to client. But I think this issue is closeable?

review_comments: nit: it'd be great to add a comment to explain why we return `false` in this case.

Would it make sense to also add a test with class inheritance where:
- a base class has a constructor with optional params (and another tests with non-optional params)
- a child class that inherits the base one has no constructor
I don't think so. The code generation involved here doesn't look at inheritance hierarchy - that's resolved at constructor call time.
